title: Class 6 Maths Linear Equations: The Balance Method Explained + Free Quiz
meta_title: Class 6 Maths Linear Equations Explained + Quiz
meta_desc: Understand class 6 maths linear equations: LHS = RHS, the balance idea, transposing, and solved word-problem case studies. Plus a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: An equation is just a balanced scale that happens to use an x. Here is how I teach the NCERT Class 6 equations chapter, from LHS = RHS to solving real word problems, with a quick quiz to test yourself.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Write x + 4 = 9 on the board and a Class 6 student will often just blurt out ‘five!’ before you finish the chalk stroke. Good instinct — but ask why and you usually get a shrug. That gap is exactly what the NCERT chapter on class 6 maths linear equations is meant to close. The goal is not to guess the missing number faster; it is to understand that an equation is a statement of balance, and to have a reliable method that still works when the numbers stop being friendly.

An equation, at its heart, is two expressions joined by an equals sign. The part on the left of the ‘=’ is the LHS (left-hand side) and the part on the right is the RHS (right-hand side). Saying LHS = RHS is a promise: whatever the two sides look like, they weigh the same. In x + 4 = 9, the LHS is x + 4 and the RHS is 9. The single letter that stands for the unknown — here x — is called the variable.

The balance idea behind every linear equation

I always start with a physical picture, because it makes the rules feel obvious rather than arbitrary. Imagine an old two-pan weighing scale, the kind still used at a Tier-2 sabzi mandi. On the left pan sits a mystery packet weighing x grams plus a 4 g weight. On the right pan sit 9 g of weights. The pans are level — that is your equals sign.

Now the golden rule: whatever you do to one pan, you must do to the other, or the balance tips. Remove 4 g from the left and you must remove 4 g from the right. The scale stays level, and now a lone packet on the left balances 5 g on the right. So x = 5. You did not guess. You kept the balance.

Solving a one-variable equation: two views of the same move

NCERT shows two routes to a solution, and they are the same idea wearing different clothes.

Doing the same thing to both sides

Take 3x − 2 = 13. Add 2 to both sides to get 3x = 15, then divide both sides by 3 to get x = 5. Every step keeps LHS = RHS true. This is the version I teach first because it never lets a child forget why it works.

Transposing (the shortcut)

Once the balance is second nature, transposing saves time. When a term crosses the equals sign, its operation flips: a term that was added becomes subtracted, one that was multiplied becomes divided. So 3x − 2 = 13 becomes 3x = 13 + 2 = 15, and then x = 15 ÷ 3 = 5. Same answer, fewer lines. My honest caveat: do not let students transpose before they can explain the balance version. Speed built on a shaky foundation collapses in Class 7.

Operation on the LHSBecomes on the RHS (transpose)Example
Add (+ 4)Subtract (− 4)x + 4 = 9 → x = 9 − 4
Subtract (− 2)Add (+ 2)x − 2 = 6 → x = 6 + 2
Multiply (× 3)Divide (÷ 3)3x = 15 → x = 15 ÷ 3
Divide (÷ 5)Multiply (× 5)x ÷ 5 = 2 → x = 2 × 5

Turning a word statement into an equation

This is where marks are won and lost. An equation is useless until you can build one from plain English (or a real situation). The routine I drill has three steps:

  • Name the unknown with a letter — ‘let the number be x’.
  • Translate the sentence into symbols, phrase by phrase — ‘3 more than’ means + 3, ‘twice’ means × 2, ‘is’ means =.
  • Solve, then read the answer back into the original sentence to check it makes sense.

Example: ‘Five more than twice a number is 17.’ Twice the number is 2x, five more is 2x + 5, and ‘is 17’ gives 2x + 5 = 17. Transpose the 5: 2x = 12, so x = 6. Read it back: twice 6 is 12, five more is 17. It holds.

Case study 1: Riya’s pocket money

Here is the kind of passage the case-study e-book is full of. Read it, then solve.

Riya saves the same amount every week. After 6 weeks she had saved ₹90 more than a friend who started with ₹30 already in her piggy bank and saved nothing. How much does Riya save each week?

Let Riya’s weekly saving be x. In 6 weeks she saves 6x. The friend has a flat ₹30. The passage says Riya’s total is ₹90 more than the friend’s, so 6x = 30 + 90. That gives 6x = 120, and dividing both sides by 6, x = 20. Riya saves ₹20 a week. Notice how the word ‘more than’ became a plain addition on the RHS.

Case study 2: An age puzzle

Arjun is 4 years older than his sister. The sum of their ages is 22. How old is each?

Let the sister’s age be x, so Arjun is x + 4. Their sum is x + (x + 4) = 22, which tidies to 2x + 4 = 22. Transpose the 4: 2x = 18, so x = 9. The sister is 9 and Arjun is 13. Add them — 22. Age problems trip students up only because they forget to name one person as x and describe the other in terms of that same x.

The mistakes I see most often

  • Changing only one side — subtracting 4 from the LHS but forgetting the RHS.
  • Forgetting to flip the sign while transposing, so + 4 wrongly stays + 4 after crossing.
  • Never checking the answer — a 10-second substitution catches almost every slip.

Now test yourself, then dig into the case studies

The quick quiz below covers exactly what we have walked through — LHS = RHS, the balance move, transposing, and forming an equation from words. Try all eight, read the explanations for any you miss, and when you want longer, exam-style practice, the printable case-study e-book with fully worked solutions is linked in the box below.

quiz.title: Class 6 Linear Equations Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on LHS = RHS, the balance method, transposing, and forming equations from word statements. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Class 6 simple linear equations in one variable

questions.q: In the equation x + 4 = 9, which part is the LHS (left-hand side)?
questions.explanation: The LHS is everything to the left of the equals sign, which is x + 4. The RHS is 9.
Subtract 7 from both sides: x = 12 − 7 = 5, keeping LHS = RHS balanced.

questions.q: When the term +5 is transposed across the equals sign, it becomes:
questions.explanation: A term that was added becomes subtracted after crossing the equals sign. So + 5 becomes − 5.

questions.q: Which equation means 'three more than twice a number is 15'?
questions.explanation: Twice a number is 2x, three more is 2x + 3, and 'is 15' gives 2x + 3 = 15.

questions.q: A pen costs ₹x. Three pens cost ₹45. Which equation fits, and what is x?
questions.explanation: Three pens cost 3x, which equals 45. Divide both sides by 3: x = 15, so each pen is ₹15.

questions.q: Meena is 5 years older than her brother. Their ages add up to 19. If the brother's age is x, which equation is correct?
questions.explanation: Meena is x + 5. The sum is x + (x + 5) = 19, which simplifies to 2x + 5 = 19.

faq.q: What is a linear equation in Class 6 maths?
faq.a: It is a statement that two expressions are equal, written as LHS = RHS, containing one variable that appears only to the first power — for example x + 4 = 9. Solving it means finding the value of the variable that keeps both sides balanced.

faq.q: What is the difference between the balance method and transposing?
faq.a: They give the same answer. The balance method does the same operation to both sides so LHS = RHS stays true; transposing is the shortcut where a term flips its operation as it crosses the equals sign. Learn the balance method first, then transpose to save time.

faq.q: How do I turn a word problem into an equation?
faq.a: Name the unknown with a letter, translate the sentence phrase by phrase into symbols ('twice' is × 2, 'more than' is +, 'is' is =), then solve and read the answer back into the original sentence to check it.

faq.q: Why should students always check their answer?
faq.a: Substituting the solution back into the original equation takes about ten seconds and catches the two commonest slips — changing only one side, and forgetting to flip a sign while transposing. If both sides come out equal, the answer is right.
